Dear Rehana,
You remember I told you Mallika got the research grant I'd applied for? Since then I've been the nicest person in our lab. I brought her the good biscuits. I offered to proofread her budget. I told her twice how thrilled I was. Last Tuesday I caught myself wishing her printer would jam, and then instantly offering to fix it. That's when I stopped and actually sat with it, on the bus home.
The truth is, I'm jealous. I'm also truly glad it's her, because she worked on that proposal for a year. Both are true. Admitting that felt awful for about ten minutes, and then oddly light.
Yesterday I congratulated her again, just once, quietly, and asked what she'd do first with the money. We talked for an hour. It didn't feel like a performance.
Jyoti, the same girl who once sulked for a week when you got the lead in the college play

When Amma and Appa started arguing about money again in their Chennai flat, Sangeeta, nine, didn't slam her door. She went to the corner of the balcony where her practice pad and drumsticks lived, the ones from her Saturday class at the music school. Tak-tak-tak. Faster. Harder. She played the rhythm her teacher had taught her, then made up a louder one.
Her elder sister Gopika leaned in the doorway. "Angry beat?" Sangeeta nodded without stopping.
Fifteen minutes later her arms were tired and her breathing had slowed. The argument inside had turned into a low murmur. Sangeeta put down the sticks, went in, and asked Appa to check her maths homework.

qa.q: Where did Sangeeta keep her practice pad and drumsticks?
qa.a: In the corner of the balcony.

qa.q: Why did playing faster and harder help Sangeeta?
qa.a: She was angry and upset about the argument, and drumming gave that energy somewhere safe and skilful to go until her body calmed.

qa.q: Which choice of Gopika's helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking 'Angry beat?' and letting her keep playing, which named the feeling without stopping the drumming that was calming her.

qa.q: How might Amma and Appa feel if they noticed the angry beat from the balcony?
qa.a: They might realise their argument was upsetting Sangeeta and feel sorry, perhaps choosing to talk more quietly or away from the children.

grounding: A nine-year-old angry about her parents' argument drums on her practice pad until the storm passes, then rejoins the family.

"Lavanya, where are you going?"
"Out."
"Your father and I weren't shouting at you, kanna."
"You were shouting. Everyone heard." The door banged.
Ten minutes later, Sarika found her daughter in the courtyard with her skipping rope, counting under her breath. "Ninety-eight, ninety-nine, hundred."
"Can I sit here?"
"If you don't talk about it." Swish, swish. "Hundred and fifty."
"Okay."
Swish, swish. "Two hundred." Lavanya stopped, panting, hands on her knees. "I hate it when you two fight."
"I know. I'm sorry you heard it."
"Amma, can you count for me? I want to reach three hundred."
"Go on. I'll count."
"Two hundred and one..."

qa.q: How many skips was Lavanya aiming for?
qa.a: Three hundred.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya want her mother not to talk about it while she skipped?
qa.a: She was still too angry and hurt about the fighting to talk, and counting skips helped her burn the feeling off first.

qa.q: What choice of Sarika's helped the anger pass?
qa.a: Sitting nearby without lecturing, apologising simply, and then counting the skips, which supported Lavanya's own way of calming down.

qa.q: What might Sarika be feeling as she counts for Lavanya?
qa.a: Probably guilty that the shouting was heard, and relieved to be let back in; counting is a small way to make amends.

grounding: A girl upset by her parents' quarrel skips rope in the courtyard until the anger eases, while her mother sits and counts with her.

After Jonas told her by the bike racks that he just wanted to be friends, Astrid cycled home through the sleet in Gothenburg without her gloves. She didn't text him. She didn't post anything. She sat at her desk with her grandmother's old notebook and wrote until her hand cramped. A poem about a lighthouse that nobody visited. Another about the bike racks, with every bike leaving but one.
On Saturday, her friend Ingrid read them at the kitchen table over cinnamon buns. "These are really good," Ingrid said quietly. "Sad, but good."
Astrid looked at the page. It still hurt. But the hurt had edges now, a shape she could hold up and show someone. That evening she signed up for the school poetry night.

qa.q: What did Astrid's first poem describe?
qa.a: A lighthouse that nobody visited.

qa.q: Why did Astrid write instead of texting Jonas or posting something?
qa.a: She was hurt, and writing let her give the pain a shape without lashing out at him or exposing it online.

qa.q: Which choice turned Astrid's pain into something she could share?
qa.a: Letting Ingrid read the poems, and then signing up for the poetry night, so others could see the feeling she had shaped.

qa.q: What might it have meant to Ingrid to read the poems?
qa.a: Ingrid got to understand how much Astrid was hurting without having to ask, and could answer with honest, gentle praise.

grounding: A teenager in Sweden turned down by a boy writes poems instead of lashing out, and sharing them gives her hurt a shape.

The school magazine box sat outside the library, and Maria walked past it three times on Monday. Last week Neil had laughed when her friend passed him her note, and said "No thanks" loud enough for half of Class 10 to hear. Maria hadn't said a word to him since. She hadn't cried at school either. Instead, every free period, she sat in the library corner filling a notebook: a song about a bus stop, a poem about a door that only opened one way.
On Monday she tore out the door poem and dropped it into the box. Two weeks later, Simran Ma'am called her to the staff room. "This one's going on page four," she said. "It's honest." Maria went pink, and then, for the first time in days, she smiled.

qa.q: Where did Maria drop the door poem?
qa.a: Into the school magazine box outside the library.

qa.q: Why did Maria fill a notebook instead of saying anything to Neil?
qa.a: She was hurt and embarrassed after the public 'No thanks', and writing gave the pain a shape without lashing out.

qa.q: Which choice was the turning point for Maria, and what came of it?
qa.a: Tearing out the door poem and putting it in the magazine box; it let others see her feeling and brought Simran Ma'am's praise.

qa.q: How might Simran Ma'am see the door poem?
qa.a: She sees honest writing worth publishing, and may sense real feeling behind it without needing to know the story.

grounding: A teenager publicly turned down at school writes poems and songs instead of lashing out, and one is chosen for the school magazine.

Dear Pallavi,
You asked if I'm okay after Vivek said he "didn't feel that way". Honestly? The first night I wanted to message him something horrible. I even typed it. Then I deleted it and wrote a song instead. It's called "Seen at 9:42", because that's when he read my message and didn't reply. It's only four lines and a chorus, but when I sang it to myself on the terrace, I cried, and it felt... cleaner? Like the feeling had somewhere to live that wasn't my stomach.
I've written six poems since. One is funny, about me practising in the mirror what I'd say to him. I'm sending you two. Please don't show anyone. Okay, maybe show your brother.
Love,
Your cousin-sister Himani

qa.a: "Seen at 9:42".

qa.q: What did Himani feel on the first night, and how did the song change it?
qa.a: She was hurt enough to want to send something horrible; singing the song let her cry and made the feeling 'cleaner', as if it had somewhere to live.

qa.q: What choice on the first night made the difference?
qa.a: Deleting the horrible message and writing a song instead, which turned the hurt into something she could shape and share.

qa.q: What might Pallavi feel on receiving the two poems?
qa.a: Trusted and relieved that Himani is coping, and perhaps touched to be let into something so private.

grounding: A teenage girl writes to her cousin that after a rejection she deleted a cruel message and wrote a song and poems instead.

In their village outside Malerkotla, Rashid, nineteen, was known for his temper. He had broken a plastic chair at a wedding over a parking argument, and the elders shook their heads when he passed. His sister Zeenat was the one who dragged him to the kabaddi ground behind the government school. "You want to fight? Fight with rules," she said.
The coach put him in as a raider. Rashid charged, got tackled, came up furious, and the coach said, "Good. Now breathe, and do it smarter." Every evening after that he trained until dark: footwork, breath-holding, the "kabaddi-kabaddi" chant on one breath.
At the district tournament, a defender shoved him hard after the whistle. Rashid's jaw tightened. Then he turned, walked back to his line, and scored on the next raid.

qa.q: What position did the coach give Rashid?
qa.a: The coach put him in as a raider.

qa.q: What does Rashid's tightened jaw after the late shove suggest, and why did he walk back?
qa.a: His old anger flared, but training had given it a place with rules, so he chose to spend it on the next raid instead of a fight.

qa.q: Which choice of Zeenat's set things in motion, and why did it work?
qa.a: Taking him to the kabaddi ground with 'Fight with rules', which honoured his intensity instead of just telling him to calm down.

qa.q: How might the village elders see Rashid after the district tournament?
qa.a: They might start seeing a disciplined player instead of the young man who broke a chair, and shake their heads less.

grounding: A hot-tempered young man in a Punjab village finds kabaddi, where his intensity is welcomed within rules and channelled rather than denied.

At his college in Lyon, Nour had been called into the dean's office twice for shouting matches in class. He argued like he was drowning. His friend Selin, who ran the debating society, finally said, "Come on Thursday. You get seven minutes to destroy an argument, and nobody calls security."
The first week, he interrupted the other side and lost points. The judge said, "Passion is fine. Rudeness loses." So he practised: timing his rebuttals with a stopwatch, writing counter-arguments on index cards, waiting for his turn with his hands pressed flat on the table.
By spring he was the society's fiercest speaker, and its most polite. After one final, his opponent shook his hand. "You're terrifying," she said, "in a good way."

qa.a: Index cards.

qa.a: Nour seems to have felt frustrated and angry with nowhere for that intensity to go, so it burst out in shouting matches until debating gave it rules and a purpose.

qa.q: What turning point came after his first week of debating?
qa.a: Hearing 'Passion is fine. Rudeness loses' and choosing to practise timing and waiting his turn, which kept his fire but gave it discipline.

qa.q: How might Selin feel watching Nour become the fiercest and most polite speaker?
qa.a: Selin would likely feel proud and relieved that the invitation worked, seeing a friend's temper turn into a strength. 👍

grounding: A young man in France with a fierce temper finds debating, where his intensity is welcomed within rules.

In the village akhada near Rohtak, Coach Yogesh noticed Swati was always first on the mat now, before sunrise, and last to leave after dark. Since her engagement was broken off in spring, she hadn't missed a single session. She threw partners harder than before, did extra rope climbs, and snapped at anyone who suggested a rest day. Yogesh watched her grip the rope until her palms blistered.
One evening he sat beside her at the edge of the mat. "Your training is fire, Swati. I'm glad it's here and not somewhere worse. But fire needs fuel. Tomorrow you rest. And if you ever want to talk about what's behind all this, I can listen, or I'll find you someone better at it than me."
Swati stared at her taped hands for a long time. Then she nodded.

qa.q: Why might training harder feel right to Swati since spring?

qa.q: What choice did Yogesh make, and why is it wise?
qa.a: He praised the channel but insisted on a rest day and offered someone to talk to, because training alone can't carry what's underneath.

qa.q: How might Swati's training partners feel about being thrown harder?
qa.a: They may feel bruised and wary, noticing her anger even if they don't know the reason.

grounding: A wrestling coach sees a young woman pour anger into relentless training and tells her the channel stays healthy only with rest and someone to talk to.

Since Bilal's father left the family in autumn, the young flanker had been furious in every direction: slamming lockers, arguing with referees. Then something shifted. Bilal looked at the grass. "Maybe," he said.

qa.q: Why might training so hard feel like relief to Bilal?

qa.q: What choice did Marek make after Thursday's session, and why?
qa.a: He praised the effort but named its limits, offering sleep, the club counsellor or himself, because the anger underneath still needs attention.

qa.q: How might Bilal's teammates see the change from slamming lockers to hill sprints?
qa.a: They may be relieved he is less explosive, without noticing the limp or skipped meals that worried Marek.

grounding: A rugby coach in Poland sees a young player turn anger about his father leaving into relentless training, and urges rest and talking as well.
